analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary public financing system with spending limits for Senate campaigns and cuts PAC money.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 1990 with 19 Democratic senators behind it, then referred to the Senate Rules Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a voluntary system for Senate campaigns: a candidate who agrees to a spending limit — roughly the lesser of $5.5 million or a formula based on the state's adult population — gets public money to run the campaign, cheap broadcast rates, and discounted mail. To qualify, a candidate must show real grassroots support: at least 75 percent of qualifying contributions from state residents, in amounts of $250 or less. It would also cap a candidate's own spending from personal wealth at $20,000, cut the maximum PAC contribution in half, cap total PAC money in Senate races, and ban unregulated 'soft money' party spending in federal elections.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who accept the limits get their Senate campaigns publicly funded, with the amount scaled to the state's population, and get the lowest broadcast rates plus discounted mail rates. Voters get more candidates freed from chasing large contributions, and the bill repeals the rule that let sitting members convert leftover campaign cash to personal use. Candidates who follow the rules also get extra public money if an opponent who refuses the limits or outside groups outspend them.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible Senate candidates receive public payments covering the full general election spending limit for major-party candidates, from a new Senate Account in the existing Presidential Election Campaign Fund.

To qualify, a candidate must raise at least $650,000 (or a smaller state-based floor) from individuals giving no more than $250 each, with at least 75 percent from in-state residents — forcing campaigns to rest on broad small donations rather than PACs or big checks.
The bill caps a candidate's personal and immediate-family campaign spending and personal loans at $20,000 per election cycle, closing the wealthy self-financed campaign route.
It cuts the maximum contribution from multicandidate PACs from $5,000 to $2,500, caps total PAC money in House and Senate races, and caps PAC money to state and national party committees.
It subjects party money spent 'in connection with a Federal election' — including voter drives and generic advertising — to federal limits and prohibitions, ending the soft-money loophole.

Participating candidates get the lowest broadcast rates in the weeks before elections, stations may not preempt their ads, and they get reduced postal rates; non-participating opponents must disclose in their ads that they did not agree to spending limits.
It repeals the exception letting Members of Congress convert excess campaign contributions to personal use, and triples the voluntary $1 tax-return check-off to $3 to fund the system.

analysis.who_pays: PACs and the organized interests that fund them lose half their per-candidate limit and a hard ceiling on total Senate giving. Wealthy candidates lose the ability to bankroll their own campaigns beyond $20,000. Broadcasters lose the right to preempt candidate ads and must sell time at the lowest rate in peak weeks. If the taxpayer check-off fund runs short, payments to candidates are prorated — the bill's answer is a voluntary $3 check-off and public education to raise participation.

drawbacks.text: Public financing depends on the voluntary tax check-off; the bill itself acknowledges the risk by requiring the IRS and FEC to run public education efforts to raise participation and by providing that payments are prorated if the Senate Account is short.

Spending limits are set by state population, so candidates in large, expensive media states face tighter effective caps, and a challenger who declines the limits — or outside groups running independent ads — can still vastly outspend a participant; the bill responds with extra public payments and raised limits only after the spending has already happened.

The bill layers on extensive new reporting: candidates must declare personal spending of $250,000 or more, report each new $10,000 increment within 24 hours, and independent spenders must file 24-hour reports identifying the candidate they intend to help or defeat, which increases compliance paperwork for campaigns and the Federal Election Commission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: taxpayers fund a slice of Senate campaigns through a voluntary check-off so candidates can stop depending on PAC and large-donor money, and in exchange campaigns accept hard spending limits. The main design weaknesses are funding adequacy — everything hinges on enough taxpayers opting in — and caps that can be outflanked by wealthy opponents or outside spending until matching money kicks in. On balance it is a coherent attempt at the problem, but it never received even a committee hearing or a floor debate in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kerry introduced the bill on April 5, 1990, joined by Sens. Joseph Biden and Bill Bradley.
Eighteen of the Senate's 55 Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among the cosponsors.
On the day of introduction the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
The bill's complete action history contains no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no vote of any kind before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing campaign money system stayed intact: PACs kept their $5,000 per-candidate limit and uncapped aggregate giving, wealthy candidates could keep self-financing, and soft-money party spending remained outside federal limits. Senators continued raising money under the old rules for another cycle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and the big-money status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were Senate Democrats (18 of 55), and no Republican support appears in the record; no opposition vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of opposition is not recorded.

industries.industry: Political action committees and organized interests
industries.note: The bill halves the PAC per-candidate limit to $2,500 and imposes hard aggregate caps on PAC money in House and Senate races and to party committees, cutting off the channel through which corporate, union, and trade-association money reaches Senate campaigns.
A $20,000 cap on personal and family spending per cycle would have ended million-dollar self-funded Senate campaigns, and candidates who decline the limits must advertise that fact.
Stations would have to sell candidate ads at the lowest unit rate in peak pre-election weeks and could no longer preempt those slots — a revenue and scheduling cost to stations.

The bill bans soft money — party spending in connection with federal elections outside federal limits — but gives state committees a new population-based contribution allowance and benefits from the publicly funded candidate broadcast access; parties' unregulated fundraising loses far more than they gain.

Eligible candidates get postage at one-quarter the standard rate for campaign mail, subsidizing a campaign vendor channel, but new conduit and secondary-payee reporting tightens disclosure of vendors' work for campaigns.
